metadata.title: Effects of social cues of artificial intelligence-powered pedagogical agents: A multilevel meta-analysis

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This paper is a multilevel meta-analysis of primary studies on AI-powered pedagogical agents, not an analysis of ILSA microdata. Therefore, there is no student-level sampling frame, no ILSA plausible-values (PV) generation, and no ILSA complex survey design to weight. The study instead uses multilevel random-effects meta-analytic estimation (restricted maximum likelihood) to pool effect sizes across studies and to account for dependence among multiple effect sizes within the same study. As a result, there are no ILSA weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT) to apply; the relevant “weighting” is inverse-variance weighting inherent to meta-analysis rather than survey weighting.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a multilevel meta-analysis synthesizing effect sizes from multiple primary studies rather than estimating student-level cognitive achievement scores from ILSA-style plausible values. Because the dependent variables are study-level outcomes (e.g., cognitive/affective/behavioral outcomes and cognitive load) extracted from published reports, PV handling is not part of the analysis pipeline. Missing-data handling is not reported because the paper does not describe an imputation strategy for individual missing observations; instead, it relies on inclusion criteria requiring sufficient summary statistics to compute effect sizes.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Included 33 studies that (1) used AI-powered pedagogical agents (with AI components or AI-driven functionality), (2) compared conditions with vs. without social cues embedded in the agents, and (3) reported sufficient statistics (e.g., sample sizes and means/SDs) to estimate effect sizes for cognitive, affective, behavioral outcomes, and/or cognitive load. Screening was conducted by two trained researchers with consensus procedures, and study quality was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist for Quasi-Experimental Studies.

data.outcome_summary: This multilevel meta-analysis (Educational Research Review, 2025) synthesizes 33 primary studies evaluating how social cues in AI-powered pedagogical agents (AIPAs) affect learning. The authors pooled a total of 185 effect sizes using a three-level random-effects meta-analytic approach (sampling error, within-study heterogeneity, and between-study heterogeneity) estimated via restricted maximum likelihood in R (metafor). Across outcomes, social cues showed statistically detectable positive effects on cognitive learning outcomes (g = 0.359, SE = 0.084, P < .001, 95% CI [0.191, 0.526]), affective learning outcomes (g = 0.519, SE = 0.147, P < .001, 95% CI [0.226, 0.812]), and behavioral learning outcomes (g = 0.458, SE = 0.139, P = .003, 95% CI [0.169, 0.746]). Cognitive load showed no detectable effect (g = 0.039, SE = 0.086, P = .663, 95% CI [−0.153, 0.230]). Moderators for cognitive outcomes included agent form, anthropomorphism, instructional setting, interaction type, and educational level; affective outcomes were moderated by publication type. Limitations include reliance on reported summary statistics from heterogeneous primary studies and no student-level PV/survey-weight framework.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is not an empirical ILSA/NAEP/PISA microdata ML study; it is a systematic multilevel meta-analysis. Consequently, there is no ILSA program/cycle/grade/domain, no student-level analytic sample, no country-level student counts, and no ML model training/evaluation on ILSA data. The “methods” are meta-analytic (effect-size computation, multilevel pooling, influence diagnostics, and publication-bias checks), so fields like PV handling, missing-data imputation, and ML techniques are not applicable in the ILSA-ML sense.
